The paper restricts the wage analysis to employed individuals with observed wages and, for several subgroup analyses, further restricts to prime-age (25–44) native-born adults with at least upper-secondary education. The manuscript does not report the specific PIAAC sampling weight variable(s) or replicate-weight procedure, so the exact weighting implementation is not documented in the text provided. For analysts replicating this work, the appropriate approach is to use PIAAC’s complex survey weights when producing population-representative estimates and to apply the corresponding variance estimation method; however, this paper’s methodological details on weights are not explicitly stated.

This is therefore a reporting gap for missing-data treatment, even if the study’s main results are based on available-case samples after standard survey processing.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The wage analysis is restricted to employed individuals for whom hourly wages are observed. For subgroup analyses of the relationship between skills/wage dispersion and educational attainment, the sample is further restricted to prime-age (25–44) native-born individuals with at least an upper secondary degree. For the parental education gradient, the estimation sample is restricted to native-born individuals and the regression controls include gender and a quadratic term in age; the paper also uses a different age-group categorisation (25–34, 35–44, 45–54, 55–65) to reduce selection bias for very young adults. The provided text does not specify additional exclusions (e.g., missing covariates) or the exact missing-data rule used.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD working paper uses PIAAC (2012) to study how measured adult cognitive proficiency (literacy and numeracy) and formal educational attainment relate to labour-market outcomes, focusing on wage inequality across countries. It first documents inequality in proficiency and hourly wages using percentile dispersion measures (e.g., 90th–10th, 90th–50th, 50th–10th) and shows that the cross-country correlation between average proficiency and its dispersion is negative. It then estimates unconditional quantile regressions of log hourly wages on education and numeracy proficiency (with demographic controls), showing that education has a stronger and more inequality-enhancing profile—especially at the top of the earnings distribution—while proficiency returns are flatter above the median. Finally, it decomposes cross-country differences in wage inequality into composition effects versus wage-structure effects using an Oaxaca–Blinder-type quantile decomposition, finding that wage-structure differences dominate and that composition explains only a limited share of cross-country wage-inequality gaps. The paper’s cross-sectional design limits causal interpretation of how institutions shape returns over time.
